extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics, literary critics, and cultivated readers of art and poetry
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic criticism of art and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for aesthetic criticism: how to perceive, analyse, and describe the impressions produced by works of art and poetry, and what qualities to attend to when judging them. Emphasises concrete, subjective impressions, temperament, formal manner, and historical/contextual characteristics (especially of the Renaissance).

rubrics_metrics.name: See the object as in itself it really is
rubrics_metrics.description: “To see the object as in itself it really is” is stated as the aim of all true criticism; the critic's first duty is accurate perception of the work itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat perception/description as primary: avoid projecting abstract theories onto the object. Approach the work with the intention of apprehending its concrete, particular qualities rather than fitting it to a universal formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and discriminate one's own impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must know "one's own impression as it really is, to discriminate it, to realise it distinctly." The critic's original facts are these subjective impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and analyse the critic's immediate responses (feelings, sensations, images). Treat these impressions as data: identify their components and be precise about what exactly the work produces in you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the pleasure produced: type, degree, and modification of the self
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: 'What is this song or picture... to ME? Does it give me pleasure? and if so, what sort or degree? How is my nature modified by its presence?'—answers to these are the primary facts for aesthetic criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not only whether the work pleases but what kind of pleasure, its intensity, and how it affects temperament, thought, or moral feeling. Use these responses to ground further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse impressions; identify the 'virtue' producing the special effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic's task is "to distinguish, analyse, and separate from its adjuncts, the virtue by which a picture... produces this special impression of beauty or pleasure, to indicate what the source of that impression is, and under what conditions it is experienced."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down the overall impression into constituent elements (tone, colour, rhythm, detail, motif, character), name the unique quality (the 'virtue') responsible, and explain how it operates within the work. Success is 'disengaging that virtue' and noting it clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete, particular definitions over abstract formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not seek a universal abstract definition of beauty; instead 'to define beauty... in the most concrete terms possible' and to find formulas that express particular manifestations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid metaphysical or overly general theorising about 'beauty'—focus on concrete instances and precise description of how specific works enact aesthetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's temperament and capacity for deep feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: What is important is not that the critic possess an abstract definition of beauty but 'a certain kind of temperament, the power of being deeply moved by the presence of beautiful objects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective criticism requires sensitivity and receptivity; cultivate the personal responsiveness necessary to perceive subtle qualities. This is a stated prerequisite rather than a moralising demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal regard for all periods and contextual evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should remember 'beauty exists in many forms... To him all periods, types, schools of taste, are in themselves equal.' The question is where the genius or sentiment of a period found receptacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works within their own historical, cultural, and stylistic contexts; avoid anachronistic standards. Seek in whom/how the period's qualities are embodied rather than comparing rawly to later/earlier models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangle essential 'virtue' from commoner or incidental elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many artists do not work 'quite cleanly'—their outstanding 'virtue' may be mixed with inferior matter; the critic must 'disengage this virtue from the commoner elements with which it may be found in combination' and 'mark the degree in which it penetrates' the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate core, transformative qualities from debris or uneven material. Assess how pervasively the creative principle permeates the work (e.g., which parts are fully 'fused' by genius and which are not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intrinsic aesthetic charm from mere antiquarian interest
rubrics_metrics.description: For an old composition to be aesthetically interesting now there must be 'a real, direct, aesthetic charm in the thing itself'; antiquarian perspective alone cannot create aesthetic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical works, ask whether they possess qualities that work on today's sensibility independently of their historical interest; avoid conflating historical curiosity with artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner and formal artistry often determine the work's value
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece 'may have a great sorrow' as subject, 'yet it claims to be a thing of joy and refreshment, to be entertained... chiefly for its manner'; manner and artistic effect are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to style, tone, choice of detail, and the formal means by which feeling is produced—evaluate whether manner enhances or undermines subject-matter and whether the work's form achieves a coherent artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring beautiful objects/motifs to sustain sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects kept constantly before the eye (e.g., the two cups, Othello's handkerchief) 'keep sensation well awake' and give refinement and a sense of fate to a narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and assess motifs and repeated objects as devices that sustain attention, unify structure, heighten symbolic resonance, and modulate feeling. Consider how repetition shapes meaning and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to musicality, rhyme, and performance in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Early songs and cantefables show attention to 'a new music... always on the point of passing into true rhyme' and often 'intended to be recited by a company...'; musicality is intrinsic to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rhythm, rhyme, assonance, cadence, and performative elements; consider how sound-patterns and intended mode of delivery contribute to meaning and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and register: tailor refinement and exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poetry (e.g., Troubadour lyrics) was 'for the few, for the elect and peculiar people'—there is a cultivated manner and delicate sweetness targeted at a refined audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether tone, diction, and sophistication suit the intended audience; recognise cultivated exclusivity as a stylistic choice that can be a virtue or a limitation depending on aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise characteristic qualities of a movement (e.g., Renaissance markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Renaissance is described by qualities such as 'care for physical beauty, the worship of the body, the breaking down of limits which the religious system of the middle age imposed on the heart and the imagination' and 'love of the things of the intellect and the imagination for their own sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying or evaluating period works, use such characteristic markers (themes, values, motifs, temperamental tendencies) as criteria to determine how fully a work expresses that movement's spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of spirit across disciplines as a marker of cultural quality
rubrics_metrics.description: An age's unity—'artists and philosophers... breathe a common air'—gives unity to its varied products; art gains 'grave dignity and influence' from participating in the best thoughts of its time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works also for their relation to contemporary intellectual currents and cross-disciplinary affinities; consider whether a work both reflects and contributes to a broader cultural spirit.
